independent_deductions: The radar right triangle has fixed perpendicular leg 30 ft, changing positive road coordinate x and range D. The car is drawn to the right of the foot moving left. D²=900+x² holds over the motion, so DDprime=xxprime; at D=50, x=40 and Dprime=-80 give xprime=-100 ft/s. Speed is the absolute value, 100 ft/s, equivalent to 750/11 mph; 65 mph equals 286/3 ft/s. The source rounded 95 ft/s comparison is sufficient, but a negative signed velocity does not literally exceed a positive speed limit.

The two explicit alternatives, D=sqrt(900+x²) and x=sqrt(D²-900), agree with implicit differentiation on the depicted positive-x branch. Division by x needs x nonzero. At the perpendicular foot, Dprime=0 for every finite road velocity, so the instantaneous range rate alone cannot recover the speed using this division. After crossing the foot a signed x or different square-root branch is required.

Instantaneous values of changing quantities must be substituted after obtaining their derivative relation; fixed constants such as 30 ft can be substituted first. Treating the momentary D=50 as a constant function would erase the required motion. The general source instruction is too broad if read as banning substitution of genuinely fixed dimensions.

The inverted conical tank has fixed full radius 4 ft and height 10 ft. Similarity in the half-section gives water radius r=(2/5)h. Water volume V=(π/3)r²h=(4π/75)h³, so net volume rate Vprime=(4π/25)h²hprime. At h=5 ft with net inflow 2 ft³/min, hprime=1/(2π) ft/min. An independent slice calculation gives cross-sectional area π(2)²=4π ft² and hprime=2/(4π), confirming both value and units.

The tank capacity is fixed, whereas differentiated V is the water volume. The generic cone drawing and initial tank-volume terminology must be interpreted with the next page’s explicit water dimensions. A rigid upright cone, horizontal free surface and net inflow are model assumptions. The solved finite rate uses 0<h<10; the ideal empty apex has singular height rate and overflow needs a new model.

The satellite diagram labels fixed vertical altitude c, horizontal ground separation L, and slant range h. Thus L²+c²=h². If c is fixed, LLprime=hhprime, and for L>0 the derivative dL/dh=h/L. The time-rate quotient Lprime/hprime additionally requires hprime nonzero. If c changes, the missing term is ccprime. For a finite increment δ, ΔL/δ=(2h+δ)/(sqrt((h+δ)²-c²)+sqrt(h²-c²)), provided both points are in the domain and δ nonzero. Its limit is h/L when L>0. With c>0, h approaching c from above makes sensitivity unbounded, so a first-order approximation is especially local near the boundary.

The mirror diagram shows a parabola-like outline, an interior point, three segments to its right branch, two upward nearly vertical rays, a horizontal Δa separation and angular Δθ marking. No equation, scale, focal parameter or unambiguous input-output definition is supplied. A unique numerical or symbolic sensitivity cannot be derived from this lecture alone. Reciprocal sensitivity requires local invertibility with a nonzero finite derivative; the drawing does not establish those hypotheses. The source only introduces the omitted problem-set application.

All five figures personally inspected in original page context. The elementary geometric and calculus checks above required no external factual lookup. The asteroid sentence supplies motivation only, not an orbital model or predictive guarantee.
